newsitem.title: JAPAN: Oil slick nears Japanese coast, threatens wildlife.
newsitem.headline: Oil slick nears Japanese coast, threatens wildlife.

text.p: Oil slicks from a sunken Russian tanker started washing ashore on the coast of northern Japan on Tuesday and clean-up crews were powerless to stop a possible environmental disaster because of bad weather.

A Maritime Safety Agency (MSA) spokesman said a 10-km (six-mile) wide oil slick broke up overnight into many smaller patches in rough seas and the first oil reached a beach at Mikuni at mid-morning on Tuesday.
The oil slicks threaten a stretch of picturesque rocky coastline known as the Noto Peninsula, about 350 km (220 miles) west of Tokyo. It is famed for shrimp, crabs and women divers known as "Ama".
"A 300-metre (330-yard) stretch of coast at Oshima has been covered with a layer of oil," Mikuni town council official Kazuya Tada told Reuters.
Tada said the affected area was rich in wildlife which would be badly affected by the slick.
"The area affected is very rocky and has abundant marine life including seaweed and shellfish. The oil is likely to have a very bad effect on the local environment," he said.
"All we can do is patrol the beaches and count the slicks coming in," said Tada.
The MSA spokesman said other slicks were heading for parts of the peninsula.
"Another group of slicks has been spotted 5.4 km (3.4 miles) from Anto, near Fukui, and they are heading straight for the coast," an MSA spokesman told Reuters.
"It's impossible to mount clean-up operations because of continuing stormy weather," he added.
Bad weather has dogged efforts to stop the oil spill since the 13,157-tonne Russian-registered Nakhodka sank and broke in two during storms in the Sea of Japan last Thursday.

The spill, already described as Japan's second-biggest, grew worse on Monday when oil started seeping from ruptured tanks in the stern of the vessel where the majority of the ship's 19,000 tonnes (133,000 barrels) of heavy fuel oil was stored.
Until the stern tanks started leaking, it was estimated about 3,700 tonnes (26,000 barrels) of oil had escaped from ruptured tanks in the ship's bow.
But MSA officials now say they did not know how much oil was heading for the coast.
"We are not sure of the volume of the leaked oil. So far we have relied on the accounts of the tanker crew but we really don't know," the spokesman said late on Monday.
More than a dozen ships as well as helicopters are involved in efforts to stop the oil from reaching the coast.
Japan's biggest oil spill was in 1971, when 7,200 tonnes (50,400 barrels) of oil spilled from a tanker that ran aground near the port city of Niigata.
Since late on Monday night, all clean-up work has stopped as high winds and towering waves stopped ships from going out to sea and helicopters from flying.
The Nakhodka was built 26 years ago and authorities said the age of the ship, which was heading to Russia from China, was probably a factor in it breaking apart in the rough seas.
The 31 crew from the tanker were rescued but the captain was still missing.
MSA officials have alerted producers of shellfish, seaweed and other sea products along the coast about extensive environmental damage from the slicks.
The Ama women divers follow a centuries-old tradition in diving for shellfish and gathering seaweed without the aid of modern breathing equipment.
